catalog_quote: §5. Pitch-accent and Stress. Pitch-accent and stress are very closely associated in Chichewa. There is a weak stress which is independent of pitch and occurs regularly on the penultimate syllable, but in many words a more energetic stress is combined with the high tonal accent on the penultimate syllable, so that the two become inseparable; and in general, the radical descriptive excepted, stress is never decidedly strong unless accompanied by this musical pitch. In emphatic expressions, for example, syllables normally of low register may be pronounced on the higher pitch and at the same time be given considerably more stress. ... In a series of syllables of high pitch the stress is greatest on the final one ... In the radical descriptive, either type of stress may occur on the final syllable. Thus, it has been considered necessary to indicate stress only in the radical descriptive, where it appears in exceptional positions. Tone is phonemically essential to the language; i. e., it is inherent in the morphological elements and must always be recognized as of grammatical and syntactical importance. There are two basic tonal distinctions in Chichewa: a high register (indicated by the acute accent) and a low register, which is unmarked. [fn. 12] Stress is indicated by the symbol (') placed after the syllable.

sweep_summary: Nyanja/Chichewa (nyan1308) is not in the catalog. Of the 11 target records (8 distinct works; Hyman & Mtenje 1999 appears four times), two ZAS Papers in Linguistics items were open and read (Downing, Mtenje & Pompino-Marschall 2004; plus the extra Downing 2008 found via Crossref), Hyman 2013 on Bantu penultimate lengthening was downloaded from the author's page, and the Downing & Pompino-Marschall 2013 NLLT abstract and the Philippson 1992 theses.fr abstract were read. Everything read agrees: Chichewa is a tone language whose only stress-like prominence is penultimate lengthening at the phonological-phrase level (culminatively extra-long on the sentence-final penult), fixed at the phrase's right edge and not attracted to focus; no source read describes lexical word stress. Hyman & Mtenje 1999 is paywalled and, per its Cambridge summary, about minimality/reduplication/tone, not stress. Not obtainable online: Downing 2003 FAB 'Stress, tone and focus in Chichewa and Xhosa' (print only; highest acquisition priority as the most on-title item), Downing 2016 Prosodic Studies (not found), Peterson 1987 CLS 23 and Mtenje 1995 LINCOM (print only; 'accent' there is almost certainly tonal accent, unverified), and Philippson's 542-page thesis (theses.fr: not accessible; unclear whether Chichewa is in its ~30-language sample).fr, HAL, archive.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Chichewa is a two-tone language (H vs unmarked L). A weak, non-contrastive stress falls regularly on the penultimate syllable; it becomes strong only when the penult also carries high tone, so stress and pitch accent are practically inseparable. Older grammars (Riddel 1880 p. 9; Henry 1891 pp. vii, 18; Hetherwick 1907 pp. 21-22) and the FSI course (1965 p. 164) all state the same penult rule, and note that enclitics (-nso, -ni, -tu, demonstratives) shift the stress to the penult of the enlarged word. Modern phonological work (Kanerva 1990 as cited; Myers 1999 pp. 215, 218; Downing 2008; Downing et al. 2004) treats the correlate as penultimate vowel lengthening whose domain is the phonological phrase, not the word: the phrase-penult is lengthened/'stressed', with the IP-final penult longest; focus does not attract it.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned by Watkins. Henry (1891) mentions in passing a 'secondary accent' on a tense-marker syllable (-na-) in one verb form; Downing (2008) describes phrase-level penult prominence with a culminative sentence-final penult, not word-internal secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Watkins: 'radical descriptive' (ideophones) may bear either type of stress on the final syllable; in the compilation of high-pitched syllables the stress is greatest on the last; emphatic pronunciation can raise pitch and stress on normally low syllables. Older grammars: enclitic particles may or may not draw the accent forward (Henry 1891 p. 18; Hetherwick 1907 p. 22). Downing & Mtenje 2017 (per Wikipedia, unverified) exempt non-Chewa names/loans from penult lengthening.
new_statements.domain_note: Watkins states the penult rule at word level but notes (p. 15) that the penult vowel is lengthened only when a word stands alone or as the last word of a 'sound group'; Kanerva 1990, Myers 1999 and Downing 2004/2008 locate lengthening/prominence at the penult of the phonological phrase (and most strongly the intonation-phrase-final penult). Scotton & Orr 1980 (Peace Corps course, p. 28) say 'syllable stress seems to be absent in Chichewa', treating the language as tone-only; the disagreement is terminological (stress vs. phrase-penult lengthening).
new_statements.identity_note: Watkins 1937 describes Chichewa, the Chewa variety of Nyanja spoken in the Kasungu, Dowa and Lilongwe districts of (then) Nyasaland — the variety Glottolog subsumes under nyan1308 (ISO nya). The older grammars (Riddel 1880, Henry 1891, Hetherwick 1907) describe the Lake Nyasa / Shire Highlands Nyanja (Mang'anja) varieties; the Kanerva/Downing work is on the Nkhotakota dialect. All agree on penult prominence.

new_statements.quote: In all three of these Bantu languages, though, the highest degree of stress (defined as vowel lengthening) in the sentence is fixed on the penult syllable of the final prosodic phrase in the sentence. Downing et al.'s (2007) exploratory phonetic study shows that penults in the sentence-final prosodic phrase are significantly lengthened in Chichewa compared to sentence-medial (non-prepausal) phrase penult vowels. The penult vowels of phrases containing focused elements are never longer than penults in sentence-final phrases.

Chichewa is a two-tone language; the only stress-like prominence is penultimate lengthening, and its domain is the phonological phrase (phrase-penult syllable), with culminative extra lengthening on the sentence-final penult. new_statements.relation_note: Same placement and type as the catalog record (Watkins 1937: weak stress regularly on the penult in a tone language) and as the Downing 2008/2010 and Hyman 2013 statements held by the project (penultimate lengthening as the only stress-like prominence). Philippson adds the comparative framing: penult prominence in Nyanja/Chewa is length-only (no pitch culmination), demarcative, in a language that retains distinctive H tones; it does not specify the domain (word vs phrase), so it neither confirms nor contradicts Downing's phrase-penult domain.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Nyanja-Chewa keeps distinctive (lexical) H prosodemes — Philippson classes it as an 'accentual' reduced-tone language with an H* melody (with question marks: graded '+' = moderately documented, second-hand data from Watkins 1937, Kanerva, Moto, Mtenje) — and in addition has a non-distinctive demarcative accent on the penultimate syllable, realised as a culmination of LENGTH (penultimate lengthening) but not of pitch. No other stress position is mentioned; the penult prominence is demarcative (word/group-final edge), not contrastive.
new_statements.exceptions: None for the penult accent. On tone: Philippson notes (p. 442) that some Chewa dialects may have neutralised the HB/HH noun-stem opposition (Watkins 1937 suggests it, unconfirmed), and that the only Nyanja dialect he has first-hand data on, Mwela of Tanzania, keeps the three patterns distinct.
new_statements.identity_note: Philippson treats 'nyanja (N31a)' and 'chewa (N31b)' together as 'nyanja-chewa', graded '+' (moderately documented) from second-hand sources (Watkins 1937 Kasungu Chewa; Kanerva 1986, Moto 1987/88, Mtenje for Malawian Chichewa); his only first-hand Nyanja data are from the Mwela dialect of Tanzania (p. 442 n.1). The statements quoted are about the language as a whole.
